https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Mobile numbers belonging to Andy Burnham’s cabinet colleagues Wes Streeting, Alex Norris and Chris Bryant were found online. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Mobile numbers belonging to Andy Burnham’s cabinet colleagues Wes Streeting, Alex Norris and Chris Bryant were found online. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images Andy Burnham Cabinet ministers’ mobile numbers found online after Burnham targeted Revelation about security leak follows person pretending to be senior White House aide contacting prime minister Kevin Rawlinson , Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu Mon 17 Aug 2026 14.25 EDT First published on Mon 17 Aug 2026 05.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least three UK cabinet ministers have had their personal mobile phone numbers published online, amid mounting concern over the security of senior politicians after Andy Burnham was targeted by an impersonation scam. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, justice secretary, Alex Norris, and Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, had their numbers available online with their names. A reference containing Streeting’s number has since been removed, a source told the Guardian, noting he does all his government business on his official government phone. Officials are understood to be working to take down the others. The leak, first revealed by Politico, come after Burnham exchanged messages with someone posing as Donald Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles. The prime minister was in contact with an unknown individual pretending to be Wiles before concerns were raised about the incident. No messages of significance were sent and the suspicious activity was quickly reported to the appropriate authorities, it is understood. The British embassy in Washington was so concerned it raised the matter with the White House, according to Politico. A UK government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on national security matters.” Downing Street refused to say whether any measures had been taken to prevent another breach happening again. No 10 refused to say whether Burnham was embarrassed that he had communicated with the imposter, and declined to say whether the messages were exchanged on WhatsApp. Last year, the Wall Street Journal reported that the FBI had launched an investigation into efforts to access Wiles’s phone after an unknown person pretending to be her contacted prominent Republicans and business chiefs. There have been security concerns related to Trump’s White House, with the president’s personal phone number common knowledge among reporters covering US politics . In December 2025, a US defence department report concluded Trump’s defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, had endangered the lives of US service personnel when he discussed details of a military operation with fellow senior US officials in a group chat to which a journalist had been added. According to a source, Hegseth violated departmental policies when he shared secret information in a Signal messaging chat. The chat was disclosed after the then national security adviser, Mike Waltz, added a journalist for the Atlantic, having saved his number under someone else’s name. Besides Waltz and Hegseth, the group also included the vice-president, JD Vance, and the CIA director, John Ratcliffe. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The source said the report by the inspector general, the internal investigative agency for the department, found the information Hegseth distributed was secret and could have put US troops in danger if it had been intercepted by an enemy force. In March, citing multiple anonymous sources the Guardian has not been able to verify, the Atlantic reported that the White House had been told Trump’s contact details had been offered for sale to people seeking influence. “It’s honestly just wild,” one of them told the outlet. “I’ve heard of CEOs offering money for his number. https://www.politico.eu/article/mark-car.text: PARIS — Mark Carney will wrap up a week spent shifting his country’s foreign policy toward Europe on Sunday with the first-ever visit by a Canadian prime minister to the obscure French territory of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, where he’ll meet President Emmanuel Macron. The trip to the picturesque archipelago — a few kilometers off the south coast of the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador and home to fewer than 6,000 people — comes after Carney travels to Strasbourg for Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union speech on Wednesday . The Canadian leader then journeys on to Liverpool to meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Carney and Macron will discuss cooperation on AI, energy, defense and critical minerals, according to a statement from the Canadian prime minister’s office. It is also Macron’s first trip there since taking office in 2017. Advertisement Advertisement While Carney has for months sought to move Ottawa closer to Brussels and Paris as part of his middle powers alliance against the U.S. under President Donald Trump, the pivot has taken on renewed urgency amid the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen each side slap reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars worth of goods . “Canada has understood that the U.S. has changed its paradigm and wants a way into the EU — the front door is Saint-Pierre and Miquelon,” said Stéphane Lenormand, an independent lawmaker who represents the archipelago in the French parliament. Saint-Pierre and Miquelon was among the many territories and sovereign states of North America that Trump covered with the U.S. flag in a Truth Social post last week, eliciting widespread condemnation in Europe . Though the trip was planned before the post went live, it reinforced the need for new partnerships “based on sovereignty, open systems, and democratic control,” said a person close to Macron, who was granted anonymity to discuss the trip’s planning. Carney said over the weekend he was looking to build a “ unique alliance ” with the EU after the publication of a Wall Street Journal report suggesting he had floated making Canada an “associate member” of the bloc — a novel status rather than an existing category of membership. The Canadian PM’s office similarly boasted of the “unique partnership” shared by France and Canada in its statement announcing the trip. There are still wrinkles to iron out in that partnership, however — including one in Saint-Pierre and Miquelon itself. Fishers on both sides of the France-Canada maritime border have squabbled for decades over access to lucrative Atlantic halibut in the overlapping waters between Newfoundland and Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. A 2024 agreement limits French fishers to catching 3% of the allowable halibut quota set by the Canadian government after complaints from industry representatives, who accused France of aggressively targeting halibut outside their territorial waters. Advertisement Advertisement Lenormand, the French lawmaker, said Carney’s pivot could give Paris the upper hand in future negotiations over fishing rights. “What’s happening with Trump is unfortunately worrying, but it gives a chance to reaffirm our geostrategic position, and that matters for the future,” he said. Milena Wälde contributed to this report.

https://www.politico.eu/article/americas.text: Democratic backsliding in Washington is damaging the international rules and alliances that underpin Europe’s security, while increasing the risk of conflict worldwide, per a new report out Tuesday. The weakening of checks and norms in the United States is putting pressure on the alliances and international rules the rest of the world relies on, while also giving governments cues to attack institutions at home, according to a new report from the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance. “Whatever happens in the U.S. has global ramifications, and I think this is one of the really big stories happening in the world today,” IDEA Secretary-General Kevin Casas-Zamora said in an interview. Advertisement Advertisement Comparing 2025 with 2020, IDEA recorded seven statistically significant declines in U.S. democratic performance, including judicial independence, access to justice, the effectiveness of parliament, press freedom and freedom of expression. Nearly half of the 30 indicators it uses to measure American democracy have fallen to their lowest levels since 1975. The erosion is unfolding against a deeply polarized backdrop. A July Lowy Institute analysis described U.S. politics as increasingly tribal, with rival camps that see each other as threatening and excuse anti-democratic behavior when it suits them. The report says U.S. President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch in 2025 and that the consequences were “far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation.” That assessment also has a concrete policy backdrop. A February 2025 executive order directed officials carrying out U.S. foreign policy to act under the president’s authority and warned that failure to implement his policy could lead to professional discipline. Casas-Zamora elaborated that the spillover was evident in the way governments justify attacks on democratic institutions and civil society. “What we are seeing is that all the countries take cues from what has happened in the U.S. in the recent past. We see it in very concrete cases,” he said. “Many of the arguments used in the U.S. when USAID was shut down were later used in Serbia, for example, to clamp down on civil society organizations that were deemed undesirable by the government,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Global security consequences The U.S. decline forms part of a broader democratic recession. In 2025, 98 of 173 countries — 57 percent — declined in at least one democratic factor over five years according to the report, while only 55 improved. It was the 11th consecutive year in which more countries saw their democratic performance deteriorate than advance. The U.S. is not an isolated case, but its size and influence make its decline especially consequential. IDEA’s central warning is that democratic erosion is also a security problem. The world recorded 65 violent conflicts in 2025, the highest number since 1946, including a record eight conflicts between countries. The report says hybrid political systems, where democratic procedures exist but political competition and enforceable rights are weak, have been involved in conflict more often than either fully authoritarian systems or well-functioning democracies. “It is the low-performing democracies that are in this really tricky spot where conditions for conflict are more likely,” Casas-Zamora said. Casas-Zamora pointed to Russia as a tangible example. “I have to think that a fully democratic Russia, with checks and balances, with freedom of the press, with civil society organizations able to organize themselves and hold public officials to account, would not have invaded Ukraine. It’s plain as that,” he added. Europe still leads the democratic rankings, but it recorded 77 declines against 42 advances between 2020 and 2025. Civil liberties, access to justice and credible elections were among the areas under greatest pressure. Germany offered a fresh illustration of that strain earlier this month, when the far-right Alternative for Germany won 43.8 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU fell to 17.2 percent, its worst-ever result in the eastern state, leaving mainstream parties scrambling to explain the AfD’s rise and keep it from power. Advertisement Advertisement Casas-Zamora said the appeal of populist-authoritarian parties cannot be reduced to hostility toward democracy. “Whether you like or dislike populist authoritarian parties and leaders and discourses, they’re a symptom of something. They are a symptom that a hell of a lot of people are not feeling represented.” Voters may care more about safe borders, safer neighborhoods and fairness than procedural arguments about democratic institutions. The answer, he said, is to treat democratic resilience as a security issue: “The protection of democracy needs to be at the heart of security agendas and not as a footnote.”
